title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a machine-generated alert was passed to officers in the field for enforcement. The system matched a plate it had misread to a stolen vehicle record, and the match was acted on as though it were correct. The failure sits at the handoff between detection and detention: the alert was treated as a sufficient basis for a stop rather than as a lead requiring confirmation.

Catching it would have required an independent check of the plate against the vehicle before officers approached, which is what the vendor itself says should happen. The reporting also attributes the misread to a tinted plate cover, meaning the input to the system was outside the conditions under which it reads reliably. A human comparison of the plate on the car with the plate in the alert would have broken the chain at either point.

What is not established is whether the deputy failed a required verification step, whether the tinted cover was in fact the cause of the misread, or whether any policy governed how such alerts must be confirmed. The sheriff's attribution of the error and his assessment that the deputy acted reasonably are statements by an interested party, not findings.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later attributed the error to an illegal tinted plate cover and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
